title: A meta systematic review of artificial intelligence in higher education: a call for increased ethics, collaboration, and rigour
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper is a tertiary review that maps and synthesizes evidence syntheses on artificial intelligence in higher education. The authors ask what kinds of AI evidence syntheses have been conducted, where they are published, who is doing the work, what methods and technologies are used, how high the review quality is, and what AI application areas and findings dominate the literature. The motivation is to provide a more rigorous, field-level picture of AI in education at a time of rapid growth and increasing public attention to generative AI.

The review searched major bibliographic databases and additional sources for English-language journal articles and conference papers published from January 2018 to July 2023 that were secondary studies on AI in formal higher or continuing education and had a method section. From 5,609 records, 66 reviews focused solely on higher education and were included for synthesis. The corpus spans a range of review types, but systematic literature reviews were most common. Most reviews addressed general AI in higher education, with substantial attention also given to profiling and prediction and adaptive systems/personalisation; fewer focused specifically on assessment/evaluation or intelligent tutoring systems.

The paper concludes that AIHEd evidence synthesis has grown quickly but is uneven in quality and reporting transparency. Common shortcomings included incomplete reporting of search methods, inter-rater reliability, coding schemes, and quality appraisal. The review also found that AI applications in higher education are most often discussed in relation to teaching and learning support, especially adaptive systems, chatbots, personalised content, and predictive uses, with comparatively less attention to administrative applications. The authors call for greater ethical scrutiny, stronger methodological rigour, and more interdisciplinary and context-sensitive research in future primary and secondary studies.

identified_tools.name: ITS (General)
identified_tools.description: A general category of intelligent tutoring systems and related AI instructional support tools that provide adaptive instruction, diagnosis, and automated feedback.
identified_tools.use_case: This paper is a tertiary review of AI in higher education and uses ITS as one of Zawacki-Richter et al.'s thematic categories for classifying reviewed evidence syntheses; it does not evaluate a single ITS product.

findings.finding_summary: Across the higher-education review corpus, only 21.2% (n=14) of evidence syntheses discussed intelligent tutoring systems. The paper characterizes ITS as AI that teaches course content, diagnoses strengths and weaknesses, offers automated personalised feedback, curates learning materials, and supports collaboration, but it does not report a pooled causal effect for literacy or any other outcome.
findings.measure: Frequency and thematic characterization of ITS-focused evidence syntheses within the review corpus

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generic category for generative AI chatbots and text-generation tools without a named product specified.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper mentions generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, DALL-E, Bard, and LLaMA in the introduction and explicitly excludes generative AI/ChatGPT-focused reviews from the included corpus; no empirical evaluation of a specific generative AI tool is conducted.

quality_tier_rationale: This is a meta-systematic review of secondary studies rather than a direct empirical evaluation of an AI tool. It provides descriptive synthesis of review characteristics and themes, not a causal study of a named product or intervention.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper has field-level relevance because it maps AI application areas and evidence quality, but it does not estimate an intervention effect on student outcomes. Any impact is indirect and interpretive rather than measured as an effect size.
